glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Jesus shows His authority to forgive sins, welcomes sinners to His table, brings the joy and newness of the Bridegroom, restores life, health, and sight, and, moved with compassion for the shepherdless crowds, tells His disciples to pray for laborers for the harvest.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Matthew 9 completes the account of Jesus’ mighty works begun in chapter 8. He returns to Capernaum, “His own city” (9:1), where opposition from religious leaders begins to grow.

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:
• Matthew 9:1–8 — Jesus Forgives and Heals a Paralytic

  • Matthew 9:9–13 — Jesus Calls Matthew and Eats with Sinners

  • Matthew 9:14–17 — The Bridegroom, New Cloth, and New Wine

  • Matthew 9:18–26 — A Ruler’s Daughter Raised and a Woman Healed

  • Matthew 9:27–31 — Two Blind Men Receive Their Sight

  • Matthew 9:32–34 — A Mute Man Delivered and Two Responses

  • Matthew 9:35–38 — Compassion for the Multitudes and Prayer for Laborers

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “But go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice.’ For I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance.’” (Matthew 9:13)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
The chapter opens with a paralyzed man carried by friends. Jesus sees their faith, the paralytic’s together with his friends’, and first says, “Son, be of good cheer; your sins are forgiven you” (9:2). When scribes call this blasphemy, Jesus heals the man so they may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. Then He calls Matthew from the tax office and eats with tax collectors and sinners. To the Pharisees He quotes Hosea: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (9:13). The Physician has come for the sick, calling sinners to repentance.

Jesus’ presence changes everything. Wedding guests do not fast while the Bridegroom is with them, and His new work cannot be patched onto old religious habits. It needs new wineskins. The restorations that follow show the same life: a ruler’s daughter raised, a woman healed after twelve years, two blind men given sight, and a mute man set free. Some marvel, while the Pharisees accuse Him of working by the ruler of demons. The chapter ends with Jesus Himself, seeing weary crowds like sheep without a shepherd, moved with compassion, and asking His disciples to pray for workers.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Matthew 9:1–8 — Jesus Forgives and Heals a Paralytic

Jesus tells a paralyzed man that his sins are forgiven, and when scribes accuse Him of blasphemy, He heals the man to show His authority to forgive. The crowds glorify God for giving such authority.

Matthew 9:9–13 — Jesus Calls Matthew and Eats with Sinners

Jesus calls Matthew the tax collector and eats with tax collectors and sinners. Answering the Pharisees, He says that the sick need a physician and that God desires mercy, not sacrifice.

Matthew 9:14–17 — The Bridegroom, New Cloth, and New Wine

Asked why His disciples do not fast, Jesus says the friends of the Bridegroom cannot mourn while He is with them, though days of mourning will come. New cloth and new wine show that His new work requires new wineskins.

Matthew 9:18–26 — A Ruler’s Daughter Raised and a Woman Healed

A ruler asks Jesus to raise his daughter, and on the way a woman with a twelve-year flow of blood touches His garment in faith. Jesus tells her that her faith has made her well, then takes the girl by the hand and she rises.

Matthew 9:27–31 — Two Blind Men Receive Their Sight

Two blind men cry out to the Son of David for mercy. Jesus asks whether they believe He can do this, touches their eyes, and they see.

Matthew 9:32–34 — A Mute Man Delivered and Two Responses

Jesus casts a demon out of a mute man, and he speaks. The crowds marvel, but the Pharisees say Jesus casts out demons by the ruler of the demons.

Matthew 9:35–38 — Compassion for the Multitudes and Prayer for Laborers

Jesus teaches, preaches, and heals in all the cities and villages. Seeing the weary crowds like sheep without a shepherd, He is moved with compassion and tells His disciples to pray the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Matthew 9 shows that Jesus’ deepest work is forgiveness. The healing of the paralytic makes visible an authority that belongs to God alone, and the table with sinners shows that His mercy reaches people others had written off. Religious knowledge can exist without mercy, and Jesus sends the Pharisees back to Hosea to learn it.

The chapter also shows where mission begins. Before Jesus sends the Twelve in chapter 10, He looks at the crowds with compassion and tells His disciples to pray. The work of the harvest grows out of His care for people and depends on His sending, not on human plans.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Authority to forgive. The Son of Man forgives sins and proves it by healing (9:2–8).

Mercy toward sinners. Jesus calls Matthew and eats with sinners, quoting Hosea 6:6 (9:9–13).

The Bridegroom’s newness. His presence brings joy and calls for new wineskins (9:15–17).

Faith that reaches Him. The paralytic and his friends, the ruler, the woman, and the blind men bring their need to Jesus (9:2, 18, 21, 28).

Compassion and harvest. Jesus’ compassion leads to prayer for laborers (9:36–38).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Blasphemy (9:3). Speaking against God or claiming what belongs to Him. The scribes understand that forgiving sins is God’s right.

Tax collectors (9:9–10). Matthew sat at a tax office collecting taxes. People in this occupation were often dishonest and were widely despised as sinners.

Bridegroom (9:15). Jesus’ picture of Himself, recalling God as Israel’s husband (Isaiah 62:5). His presence is a time of joy.

New wine and new wineskins (9:17). Fresh wine expanded as it fermented and needed flexible skins. Jesus’ new work calls for hearts and fellowships that are soft and open, not hardened by religious routine.

Son of David (9:27). A title for the promised Messiah from David’s line. The blind men call Jesus by it as they ask for mercy.

Moved with compassion (9:36). A deep inward stirring of pity that leads to action. It is what moves Jesus toward the crowds.

focus: Matthew 9 completes the account of Jesus’ mighty works by showing His authority to forgive sins, His call of Matthew the tax collector, and His mercy toward sinners. The chapter continues with the question about fasting, the raising of a ruler’s daughter, and the healing of a woman, two blind men, and a mute man, and it ends with Jesus moved with compassion for the multitudes and telling His disciples to pray for laborers in the harvest.

sections.title: Jesus Forgives and Heals a Paralytic
sections.summary: When people bring Him a paralytic, Jesus says, “Son, be of good cheer; your sins are forgiven you” (Matthew 9:2), and some scribes accuse Him of blasphemy. To show “that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins” (Matthew 9:6), Jesus commands the man to rise and go home, and the multitudes glorify God.

sections.title: Jesus Calls Matthew and Eats with Sinners
sections.summary: Jesus calls Matthew from the tax office with the words “Follow Me” (Matthew 9:9), and many tax collectors and sinners sit down with Him and His disciples. When the Pharisees object, Jesus answers that the sick need a physician and tells them to learn what this means: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13).

sections.title: The Bridegroom, New Cloth, and New Wine
sections.summary: When John’s disciples ask why Jesus’ disciples do not fast, He answers that the friends of the bridegroom cannot mourn while the bridegroom is with them, though they will fast when He is taken away. He adds that no one puts unshrunk cloth on an old garment or new wine into old wineskins, but new wine is put into new wineskins and both are preserved.

sections.title: A Ruler’s Daughter Raised and a Woman Healed
sections.summary: A ruler asks Jesus to come and lay His hand on his daughter, who has just died, and on the way a woman with a flow of blood for twelve years touches the hem of His garment, and Jesus tells her, “Be of good cheer, daughter; your faith has made you well” (Matthew 9:22). Jesus then enters the ruler’s house, takes the girl by the hand, and she arises, and the report goes out into all that land.

sections.title: Two Blind Men Receive Their Sight
sections.summary: Two blind men follow Jesus, crying out, “Son of David, have mercy on us!” (Matthew 9:27), and He asks whether they believe He is able to do this. He touches their eyes, saying, “According to your faith let it be to you” (Matthew 9:29), and their eyes are opened, but though He sternly warns them to tell no one, they spread the news about Him.

sections.title: A Mute Man Delivered and Two Responses
sections.summary: When a mute, demon-possessed man is brought to Jesus, the demon is cast out and the mute man speaks. The multitudes marvel that nothing like this was ever seen in Israel, but the Pharisees say that He casts out demons by the ruler of the demons.

sections.title: Compassion for the Multitudes and Prayer for Laborers
sections.summary: Jesus goes about all the cities and villages teaching, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every sickness and every disease. Moved with compassion because the multitudes are weary and scattered “like sheep having no shepherd” (Matthew 9:36), He tells His disciples to pray the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into His harvest.

1.brief: Jesus gets into a boat, crosses over, and comes to His own city, Capernaum. Having been sent away from the Gergesene region, He returns to the town where He has made His home.
1.explain:
“So He got into a boat, crossed over, and came to His own city.”

The people of the Gergesene region had begged Jesus to leave (8:34). He does not force Himself on them. He crosses the Sea of Galilee and returns to “His own city.” This is Capernaum, the town where He made His home after leaving Nazareth (4:13).
1.notes: Mark 2:1 places the healing that follows in Capernaum, in a house where Jesus was staying.

2.brief: People bring Him a paralyzed man lying on a bed, and seeing their faith, Jesus tells him, “Son, be of good cheer; your sins are forgiven you.” He sees the persistent trust of the man and those who carried him, and He meets the man’s deepest need first.
2.explain:
“Then behold, they brought to Him a paralytic lying on a bed.”

A man who cannot walk is carried to Jesus on a “bed,” probably a mat or stretcher. He cannot come by himself, so others bring him.

“When Jesus saw their faith,”

Jesus sees “their faith.” It includes the man and the friends who carried him. Mark and Luke add that they opened the roof to lower him down when the crowd blocked the door (Mark 2:3–4; Luke 5:18–19). Their trust in Jesus refused to give up when obstacles stood in the way.

The friends’ faith brought the man to Jesus. It did not take the place of his own relationship with God. Jesus speaks to the man himself.

“He said to the paralytic, ‘Son, be of good cheer; your sins are forgiven you.”

Jesus speaks tenderly. He calls the man “Son” and tells him to take courage. Then He says something no one expected: “your sins are forgiven you.” The man came for healing. Jesus meets his deepest need first.

Jesus does not say that this man’s sin caused his paralysis. Scripture does not treat every illness as the result of a particular sin (John 9:1–3). Here, forgiveness comes first because every person’s greatest need is to be made right with God.
2.notes: The Greek word translated “be of good cheer” means take courage. Jesus uses the same word in 9:22 and 14:27.

3.brief: Some of the scribes say to themselves, “This Man blasphemes!” They recognize that Jesus is claiming to do what only God can do, and they judge Him guilty of dishonoring God.
3.explain:
“And at once some of the scribes said within themselves,”

The “scribes” were experts in the law of Moses. They do not speak out loud. They react “within themselves.”

“This Man blasphemes!”

Their thought is an accusation. To blaspheme is to dishonor God. The scribes understand that only God can forgive sins against Himself (Mark 2:7). They see that Jesus is claiming to do what belongs to God alone. Since they do not believe He is God, they conclude He is guilty of dishonoring God.
3.notes: Under the law, blasphemy was punishable by death (Leviticus 24:16). This is the first time in Matthew that this charge is raised against Jesus. It will be raised again at His trial (26:65).

4.brief: Knowing their thoughts, Jesus asks why they think evil in their hearts. He reveals that He knows what is hidden in the heart.
4.explain:
“But Jesus, knowing their thoughts,”

The scribes spoke only in their hearts, but Jesus knows what they are thinking. Scripture teaches that God alone knows the hearts of all people (1 Kings 8:39). Jesus’ knowledge of their thoughts supports the very claim they are rejecting.

“said, ‘Why do you think evil in your hearts?”

Jesus brings their hidden thoughts into the open. He calls them “evil.” They are condemning the One who has come to forgive.
4.notes: The Greek word translated “knowing” can also be translated seeing. Some manuscripts read seeing their thoughts.

5.brief: Jesus asks which is easier to say, “Your sins are forgiven you,” or “Arise and walk.” Anyone can claim to forgive unseen sins, but a command to walk can be tested immediately.
5.explain:
“For which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Arise and walk’?”

Jesus asks a question that exposes their thinking. Saying either sentence is equally easy. But one can be checked and the other cannot. Anyone could claim to forgive sins, because no one can see whether sins have been forgiven. A command to “Arise and walk” would be proved true or false in front of everyone.
5.notes: Both forgiving sins and healing require God’s power. The question concerns which claim can be seen and tested.

6.brief: So that they may know “the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins,” Jesus tells the paralyzed man to get up, take his bed, and go home. The visible healing confirms His invisible authority to forgive.
6.explain:
“But that you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins’—”

Jesus states the purpose of what He is about to do. He wants them to know that “the Son of Man” has authority to forgive sins “on earth.” God forgives from heaven. Jesus claims to exercise that same authority here, in person.

“Son of Man” is Jesus’ favorite title for Himself. It draws on Daniel 7:13–14, where one like the Son of Man receives authority and an everlasting kingdom from God.

“then He said to the paralytic, ‘Arise, take up your bed, and go to your house.”

Jesus turns from the scribes to the paralyzed man and gives three commands. Get up. Pick up the mat that carried you. Go home. The man who was carried in will walk out carrying his own bed.
6.notes: The Greek word translated “power” means authority, the right and power to act.

7.brief: The man gets up and goes home. Jesus’ word proves true, and with it His claim to forgive sins.
7.explain:
“And he arose and departed to his house.”

The man does exactly what Jesus told him. He gets up and goes home. The healing is immediate and complete.

The visible healing proves the invisible forgiveness. If Jesus’ word could make a paralyzed man walk, His word of forgiveness was just as real.
7.notes: Mark 2:12 adds that the man went out in the presence of them all.

8.brief: When the crowds see it, they marvel and glorify God, “who had given such power to men.” They recognize God’s work in Jesus, though they do not yet grasp who He is.
8.explain:
“Now when the multitudes saw it, they marveled and glorified God,”

The crowds are amazed, and they give glory to God. They recognize that God has done this.

“who had given such power to men.”

They praise God for giving such authority “to men.” They see God at work in Jesus, but they do not yet grasp who He is. Jesus is not merely a man to whom God has lent power. He is the Son of Man who has authority to forgive sins.
8.notes: Some manuscripts read feared instead of marveled.

9.brief: Passing on, Jesus sees a man named Matthew sitting at the tax office and says, “Follow Me,” and Matthew gets up and follows Him. Jesus calls a tax collector, a man despised by his people, and Matthew leaves his post at once.
9.explain:
“As Jesus passed on from there, He saw a man named Matthew sitting at the tax office.”

The man Jesus notices is the writer of this Gospel. He was sitting “at the tax office,” a booth where taxes or tolls were collected, probably on goods moving through Capernaum.

Tax collectors worked for the ruling powers and often took more than was owed. Many Jews regarded them as traitors and sinners. Matthew records his own calling without trying to hide what he had been.

“And He said to him, ‘Follow Me.’ So he arose and followed Him.”

Jesus gives a simple call: “Follow Me.” Matthew responds at once. He leaves his booth and his income and goes with Jesus. Luke 5:28 adds that he left all.
9.notes: Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27 call him Levi. Many people in that time had two names. The list of apostles in 10:3 identifies him as Matthew the tax collector.

10.brief: As Jesus reclines at table in the house, many tax collectors and sinners come and eat with Him and His disciples. Jesus welcomes into His fellowship people others shunned.
10.explain:
“Now it happened, as Jesus sat at the table in the house,”

Jesus is at a meal “in the house.” Luke 5:29 says that Matthew gave a great feast for Jesus in his own house.

“that behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and sat down with Him and His disciples.”

Matthew’s guests include people others avoid. “Sinners” describes people known for breaking God’s law or living outside the religious customs of the community. Matthew’s friends are people like him. Jesus welcomes them to His table.

In that culture, eating together expressed acceptance and friendship. By sharing the meal, Jesus shows them that He has come for them.
10.notes: The Greek word translated “sat” means to recline. Guests at a formal meal reclined on couches around a low table.

11.brief: Seeing this, the Pharisees ask His disciples, “Why does your Teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” They see Jesus’ table fellowship with sinners as a scandal.
11.explain:
“And when the Pharisees saw it,”

The “Pharisees” were a group that was devoted to careful observance of the law and of traditions about purity. They kept apart from people they considered unclean.

“they said to His disciples, ‘Why does your Teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?”

They do not ask Jesus directly. They ask His disciples. Their question is an objection. To them, a true teacher of God would not share a table with such people. They see His fellowship with sinners as a scandal.
11.notes: Luke 15:2 records the same complaint: “This Man receives sinners and eats with them.” Jesus answers it with the parables of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son.

12.brief: Jesus answers that the healthy do not need a physician, but the sick do. He has come as a physician to people who know they need healing.
12.explain:
“When Jesus heard that,”

Jesus answers the question Himself.

“He said to them, ‘Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.”

Jesus uses a simple picture. A doctor goes to the sick, not to the healthy. Jesus compares Himself to a “physician.” He has come to people who need healing. The tax collectors and sinners know they are sick. The Pharisees think they are well.

Jesus is not saying the Pharisees have no need of Him. Everyone needs the Physician. But only those who recognize their need will come to Him for healing.
12.notes: The image of God as healer appears in Exodus 15:26: “For I am the LORD who heals you.”

13.brief: Jesus tells them to go and learn what Hosea 6:6 means, “I desire mercy and not sacrifice,” for He came to call sinners, not the righteous, to repentance. God values mercy above religious observance, and Jesus extends that mercy by calling sinners to turn to Him.
13.explain:
“But go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice.”

Jesus sends the Pharisees back to Scripture. “Go and learn” was a phrase teachers used to send students to study a text. The Pharisees knew the law well, but they had not grasped this verse. It comes from Hosea 6:6.

God commanded sacrifices, but He never wanted religious ritual without a merciful heart. Mercy is God’s own stated priority. The Pharisees kept the rules of separation but showed no mercy to those who needed God most.

“For I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance.”

Jesus states His mission. He came “to call” sinners “to repentance,” to turn from sin to God. His mercy welcomes sinners. His call also changes them.

Those who think they are already “righteous” do not see their need for the call. Jesus’ words are an invitation to everyone who knows he is a sinner.
13.notes:
Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6 again in 12:7.

Some manuscripts do not include the words to repentance in this verse. Luke 5:32 includes them.

14.brief: John’s disciples ask Jesus why they and the Pharisees fast often but His disciples do not. They wonder why Jesus’ followers do not share their practice of devotion.
14.explain:
“Then the disciples of John came to Him,”

The followers of John the Baptist come with a question. John had called Israel to repentance and lived a life of self-denial (3:4).

“saying, ‘Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but Your disciples do not fast?”

They notice a difference. They and the Pharisees “fast often,” going without food as an act of devotion. Jesus’ disciples do not. They want to know why.
14.notes: The law required fasting only on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29–31). The Pharisees fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12).

15.brief: Jesus answers that the bridegroom’s friends cannot mourn while the bridegroom is with them, but when he is taken away, then they will fast. His presence brings the joy of a wedding, and His coming departure points toward His death.
15.explain:
“And Jesus said to them, ‘Can the friends of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them?”

Jesus answers with a wedding picture. The bridegroom’s friends were the guests closest to him. A wedding was a time of joy and feasting that could last a week. No one would fast or mourn during it.

Jesus is the bridegroom. In the Old Testament, God pictured Himself as the bridegroom of His people (Isaiah 62:5). Jesus’ presence brings that joy. This is not a time for mourning.

“But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them,”

The joy will be interrupted. This is the first hint in Matthew of Jesus’ death. He will be taken from His disciples by force.

“and then they will fast.”

When He is taken away, the disciples will grieve and fast. Fasting has a place in the life of His followers (6:16–18). It fits a time of longing for Him.
15.notes:
John the Baptist also called Jesus the bridegroom and himself the friend of the bridegroom (John 3:29). Revelation 19:7 pictures the marriage of the Lamb at the end of the age.

The Greek phrase translated “friends of the bridegroom” is literally the sons of the bridechamber.

16.brief: No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, because it pulls away and makes the tear worse. Jesus has not come to patch new life onto old religious forms.
16.explain:
“No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment;”

Jesus uses a picture from everyday life. “Unshrunk cloth” is new fabric that has not been washed. Sewing it onto “an old garment” would be a mistake.

“for the patch pulls away from the garment, and the tear is made worse.”

When the garment is washed, the new patch shrinks. It pulls on the old cloth around it and tears it further.

Jesus has not come to patch something new onto an old way of life. He does not add a little grace to a system of works. What He brings requires something new from the inside out.
16.notes: Luke 5:36 records a related form of the saying, in which the new garment is also torn to make the patch.

17.brief: Nor does anyone put new wine into old wineskins, or they burst and both are lost; new wine goes into new wineskins, and both are preserved. The new life Jesus brings by His Spirit requires people made new, soft and yielded to God, rather than rigid religious routine that cannot contain it.
17.explain:
“Nor do they put new wine into old wineskins, or else the wineskins break, the wine is spilled, and the wineskins are ruined.”

“Wineskins” were containers made of animal skin. As new wine fermented, it expanded. A new skin could stretch. An old skin had become dry and stiff. It would burst, and both the wine and the skin would be lost.

“But they put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.”

New wine needs “new wineskins.” The new wine pictures the fresh and expanding work Jesus brings by His Spirit and the gospel of grace. The wineskins picture the people who receive it, individual believers and the communities they form.

A new wineskin is soft and flexible. It has been made new through death to self. It stays open to God and stretches as He works. A hardened religious routine cannot hold what Jesus brings. It bursts under the pressure of the Spirit’s work.

Jesus did not come to throw away the Scriptures (5:17). He came to fulfill God’s purpose and to make His people new (2 Corinthians 5:17). The warning is against letting good spiritual practices become religious pride or resisting the Spirit’s work because we prefer what is familiar.
17.notes: Mark 2:22 and Luke 5:37–39 record the same saying. Luke adds that no one who has drunk old wine immediately desires new, because he says the old is better.

18.brief: As Jesus is speaking, a ruler comes, worships Him, and says, “My daughter has just died, but come and lay Your hand on her and she will live.” His request goes beyond healing; he trusts Jesus to restore life itself.
18.explain:
“While He spoke these things to them, behold, a ruler came and worshiped Him,”

Jesus is still speaking when “a ruler” comes to Him. Mark and Luke name him Jairus and say he was a ruler of the synagogue (Mark 5:22; Luke 8:41). He was a respected leader in the town. He kneels before Jesus.

“saying, ‘My daughter has just died, but come and lay Your hand on her and she will live.”

In Matthew’s shorter account, the father says his daughter “has just died.” Mark and Luke tell the story in more detail, with the news of her death arriving while Jesus was on the way (Mark 5:23, 35). Matthew summarizes the whole account.

The father asks Jesus to “lay Your hand on her.” He believes that if Jesus touches her, “she will live.” He trusts Jesus to restore life itself.
18.notes: The Greek word translated “worshiped” describes bowing down or kneeling before someone in reverence.

19.brief: Jesus gets up and goes with him, and so do His disciples. Jesus responds to the father’s plea without hesitation.
19.explain:
“So Jesus arose and followed him, and so did His disciples.”

Jesus responds immediately. He gets up from the meal and goes with the father. His disciples go too.
19.notes: Jesus is following the ruler here, the reverse of 9:9, where Matthew followed Jesus.

20.brief: On the way, a woman who has suffered from bleeding for twelve years comes up behind Jesus and touches the hem of His garment. Her long illness had made her ceremonially unclean, so she approaches quietly from behind.
20.explain:
“And suddenly, a woman who had a flow of blood for twelve years”

On the way, a woman approaches. She has suffered from bleeding “for twelve years.” Mark 5:26 adds that she had spent everything on doctors and had only grown worse.

Under the law, this condition made her ceremonially unclean (Leviticus 15:25–27). Anyone she touched would also become unclean. For twelve years she had lived on the edge of community and worship.

“came from behind and touched the hem of His garment.”

She comes quietly “from behind.” She does not want to be noticed. She touches “the hem of His garment.” This was probably one of the tassels that Jewish men wore on the corners of their outer garment (Numbers 15:38–39).
20.notes: The Greek word translated “hem” can refer to the edge of a garment or to the tassels commanded in the law.

21.brief: The suffering woman tells herself, “If only I may touch His garment, I shall be made well.” Her reaching out comes from trust that Jesus can heal her.
21.explain:
“For she said to herself, ‘If only I may touch His garment, I shall be made well.”

Matthew reveals what she was thinking. She is convinced that Jesus can heal her. Her reaching out expresses her trust in Him.

The touch itself was not a technique that forced Jesus to act. Her action expressed her reliance on Him. Faith is the persuasion that God is who He has revealed Himself to be and that He will do what He has promised.
21.notes: The Greek verb translated “made well” is the word usually translated save. It can mean to rescue, heal, or make whole.

22.brief: Jesus turns, sees her, and says, “Be of good cheer, daughter; your faith has made you well,” and she is healed from that hour. He does not let her slip away unnoticed but personally welcomes and restores her, calling her “daughter.”
22.explain:
“But Jesus turned around, and when He saw her He said,”

Jesus does not let her slip away unnoticed. He turns and looks at her.

“Be of good cheer, daughter; your faith has made you well.”

He speaks to her personally. He calls her “daughter,” a word of tenderness and belonging. Her illness had lasted twelve years, and under the law it made her ceremonially unclean (Leviticus 15:25–27). Jesus does not let her go unnoticed. He addresses her personally and welcomes her.

He tells her that her “faith” has made her well. It was not the cloth that healed her. It was Jesus, whom she trusted.

“And the woman was made well from that hour.”

The healing is immediate and lasting.
22.notes: Jesus says be of good cheer both to the paralytic in 9:2 and to the woman here.

23.brief: Arriving at the ruler’s house, Jesus sees the flute players and the noisy crowd wailing. The mourning has already begun, as is customary after a death.
23.explain:
“When Jesus came into the ruler’s house,”

Jesus arrives at the home of the ruler whose daughter has died.

“and saw the flute players and the noisy crowd wailing,”

The mourning has already begun. “Flute players” were hired to play funeral music. Professional mourners would wail loudly. These customs were expected at a death, even in a poor family.
23.notes: A later Jewish writing says that even the poorest man in Israel should hire at least two flute players and one wailing woman for his wife’s funeral.

24.brief: Jesus tells them, “Make room, for the girl is not dead, but sleeping,” and they laugh at Him. For Jesus, her death is like sleep from which He can wake her.
24.explain:
“He said to them, ‘Make room, for the girl is not dead, but sleeping.”

Jesus tells the mourners to leave. He says the girl “is not dead, but sleeping.” He does not mean that she is unconscious. She is truly dead. For Jesus, her death is like sleep, because He is about to wake her.

The New Testament often speaks of the death of believers as sleep, because they will be raised (John 11:11–14; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14).

“And they ridiculed Him.”

The mourners laugh at Him. They know she is dead. They do not know who Jesus is.
24.notes: Luke 8:53 adds that they laughed because they knew she was dead.

25.brief: When the crowd has been put outside, Jesus goes in, takes the ruler’s daughter by the hand, and the girl gets up. Jesus raises the dead with a touch.
25.explain:
“But when the crowd was put outside,”

Jesus sends out the mocking crowd. Mark 5:40 says He took only the child’s parents and three disciples into the room.

“He went in and took her by the hand, and the girl arose.”

Jesus takes the dead girl “by the hand.” Touching a corpse made a person unclean (Numbers 19:11). But Jesus’ touch brings life. The father had asked Him to lay His hand on her (9:18). Jesus does, and she gets up.
25.notes: Mark 5:41 preserves Jesus’ words in Aramaic: “Talitha, cumi,” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, arise.”

26.brief: News of the girl’s rising spreads throughout that land. Jesus’ power over death cannot be kept quiet.
26.explain:
“And the report of this went out into all that land.”

The news spreads everywhere. A girl who was dead is alive. Jesus’ power over death cannot be kept quiet.
26.notes: This is the first account in Matthew of Jesus raising the dead. Raising the dead is one of the signs He sends to John in 11:5.

27.brief: As Jesus leaves, two blind men follow Him, crying, “Son of David, have mercy on us!” They recognize Him as David’s promised heir and appeal to His mercy.
27.explain:
“When Jesus departed from there, two blind men followed Him,”

As Jesus leaves the ruler’s house, two blind men follow Him.

“crying out and saying, ‘Son of David, have mercy on us!”

They call Him “Son of David.” This was a title for the Messiah, the promised King from David’s family (2 Samuel 7:12–16). These blind men see more clearly than many with sight. They recognize who Jesus is. They ask for “mercy.”
27.notes: Matthew records another healing of two blind men who call Jesus Son of David near Jericho (20:29–34).

28.brief: When Jesus enters the house, the two blind men come to Him, and He asks, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They answer, “Yes, Lord.” Jesus draws out their trust in His power before He heals them.
28.explain:
“And when He had come into the house, the blind men came to Him.”

The blind men persist. Jesus does not answer them on the road, and they follow Him into the house.

“And Jesus said to them, ‘Do you believe that I am able to do this?’ They said to Him, ‘Yes, Lord.”

Jesus asks them directly whether they trust His power. He draws out their trust in Him before He acts. They answer, “Yes, Lord.”
28.notes: The Greek word translated “Lord” can be a respectful title like sir. On the lips of those who recognize Jesus as the Son of David, it carries more weight.

29.brief: Jesus touches the blind men’s eyes, saying, “According to your faith let it be to you.” Their trust in Him receives what it asked for.
29.explain:
“Then He touched their eyes,”

Jesus touches the blind men’s eyes.

“saying, ‘According to your faith let it be to you.”

Jesus grants what they believed He could do. Their faith rested on Him. He does not mean that the strength of their faith decides the outcome. Jesus Himself heals them, in response to their trust.
29.notes: Jesus spoke in a similar way to the centurion: “as you have believed, so let it be done for you” (8:13).

30.brief: The two men’s eyes are opened, and Jesus sternly warns them, “See that no one knows it.”
30.explain:
“And their eyes were opened.”

The men can see.

“And Jesus sternly warned them, saying, ‘See that no one knows it.”

Jesus gives them a firm command not to tell anyone. He had given a similar command to the leper (8:4). Jesus may have wanted to avoid crowds who sought only miracles or who expected a political Messiah. His time to be publicly revealed had not yet come.
30.notes: The Greek verb translated “sternly warned” is a strong word. It expresses intense feeling.

31.brief: Despite His warning, the healed men go out and spread the news about Jesus throughout that region.
31.explain:
“But when they had departed, they spread the news about Him in all that country.”

The men do not obey. They tell everyone what Jesus has done. Their gratitude is understandable, but they disregard His command.
31.notes: Mark 1:45 records the same response from the leper whom Jesus told not to speak.

32.brief: As the two healed men leave, people bring Jesus a man who is mute and demon-possessed. In this case Matthew links the man’s inability to speak to demonic oppression.
32.explain:
“As they went out, behold, they brought to Him a man, mute and demon-possessed.”

As the two healed men leave, others bring a man who cannot speak. He is also “demon-possessed.” In this case Matthew links the man’s inability to speak with demonic oppression.

Not every case of muteness in Scripture is caused by a demon. Matthew identifies the cause in this particular scene.
32.notes: The Greek word translated “mute” can also mean deaf. Here the man’s silence is the focus, since he speaks after the demon leaves.

33.brief: When the demon is cast out, the mute man speaks, and the crowds marvel, “It was never seen like this in Israel!” The people recognize something unprecedented in Jesus’ works.
33.explain:
“And when the demon was cast out, the mute spoke.”

Jesus casts out the demon, and the man speaks immediately.

“And the multitudes marveled, saying, ‘It was never seen like this in Israel!”

The crowds are astonished. They have never seen anything like this. In the course of chapters 8 and 9, Jesus has healed every kind of disease, calmed a storm, cast out demons, forgiven sins, and raised the dead.
33.notes: Isaiah 35:5–6 promised that in the day of God’s salvation the tongue of the mute would sing.

34.brief: But the Pharisees say, “He casts out demons by the ruler of the demons.” The same deliverance that amazes the crowds hardens the Pharisees into attributing Jesus’ work to Satan.
34.explain:
“But the Pharisees said, ‘He casts out demons by the ruler of the demons.”

The Pharisees see the same miracle and draw the opposite conclusion. They claim that Jesus casts out demons by the power of “the ruler of the demons,” Satan himself. The work that amazes the crowds hardens the Pharisees.

This charge will return in 12:24, where Jesus answers it at length.
34.notes: In 10:25 Jesus tells His disciples that if they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, they will say the same of those of his household.

35.brief: Jesus goes through all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every sickness and disease. Matthew repeats the summary of Matthew 4:23, framing the words and works of chapters 5–9.
35.explain:
“Then Jesus went about all the cities and villages,”

Matthew gives a summary of Jesus’ ministry. He goes everywhere, to “all the cities and villages.”

“teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every sickness and every disease among the people.”

Jesus does three things. He teaches in the synagogues. He preaches “the gospel of the kingdom,” the good news that God’s rule has come near. He heals every kind of sickness.

This verse repeats almost word for word the summary of 4:23. The two summaries frame chapters 5–9. Chapters 5–7 record Jesus’ teaching. Chapters 8–9 record His mighty works.
35.notes: Matthew 4:23: “And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing all kinds of sickness and all kinds of disease among the people.”

36.brief: When Jesus sees the crowds, He is moved with compassion, because they are weary and scattered, “like sheep having no shepherd.” He sees people harassed and helpless without true spiritual leaders, and His heart goes out to them.
36.explain:
“But when He saw the multitudes, He was moved with compassion for them,”

Jesus looks at the crowds and feels deep compassion. The Greek word describes a feeling that moves the whole inner being.

“because they were weary and scattered, like sheep having no shepherd.”

He sees the people as “weary and scattered.” They are worn out and helpless. They are “like sheep having no shepherd,” with no one to guide, feed, or protect them. Their religious leaders had failed to care for them.

In Ezekiel 34, God condemned Israel’s shepherds for neglecting His flock and promised to seek His scattered sheep Himself (Ezekiel 34:11–16). Jesus is that Shepherd.
36.notes: Numbers 27:17 uses the same picture, when Moses asks God to appoint a leader so that the congregation of the LORD may not be like sheep which have no shepherd.

37.brief: Jesus tells His disciples, “The harvest truly is plentiful, but the laborers are few.” Many people are ready to be gathered into God’s kingdom, but there are few workers.
37.explain:
“Then He said to His disciples, ‘The harvest truly is plentiful, but the laborers are few.”

Jesus changes the picture from sheep to a harvest. The crowds are a field ready to be gathered. “The harvest truly is plentiful.” But there are not enough workers.
37.notes: In John 4:35 Jesus tells His disciples to lift up their eyes and look at the fields, for they are already white for harvest.

38.brief: Therefore they are to pray the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into His harvest. Mission begins with prayer to God, who owns the harvest, and this prayer prepares for Jesus sending out the Twelve.
38.explain:
“Therefore pray the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into His harvest.”

Jesus’ answer to the need is prayer. The disciples are to ask “the Lord of the harvest,” God Himself, to “send out laborers.” The harvest belongs to Him. He alone can send the workers.

This prayer leads directly into chapter 10. The disciples who are told to pray for laborers become the laborers Jesus sends. Mission begins with the Lord’s compassion and with prayer.
38.notes:
Luke 10:2 records the same command before Jesus sends out the seventy.

The Greek verb translated “send out” is a strong word. It can mean to drive out or thrust out.
